```{r setup}
sig_stars <- function(p) {
  case_when(
    is.na(p) ~ "",
    p < 0.01 ~ "***",
    p < 0.05 ~ "**",
    p < 0.10 ~ "*",
    TRUE ~ ""
  )
}

fmt_p <- function(p) {
  ifelse(is.na(p), NA_character_,
         ifelse(p < 0.0001, "<0.0001", as.character(round(p, 4))))
}

extract_coef_table <- function(coeftest_obj, keep = NULL) {
  df <- as.data.frame(unclass(coeftest_obj))
  df$Variable <- rownames(df)
  out <- df %>%
    rename(SE = `Std. Error`, p_raw = `Pr(>|t|)`) %>%
    mutate(
      Coef  = round(Estimate, 4),
      SE    = round(SE, 4),
      p     = fmt_p(p_raw),
      Sig   = sig_stars(p_raw)
    ) %>%
    select(Variable, Coef, SE, p, Sig)
  if (!is.null(keep)) out <- filter(out, Variable %in% keep)
  out
}

# Holm correction helper
holm_adjust <- function(p_vec) {
  p.adjust(as.numeric(p_vec), method = "holm")
}
```

# Introduction

Environmental, social, and governance considerations have moved from corporate finance into mainstream tourism policy. Destination management organisations, national tourism boards, and supranational agencies increasingly treat ESG progress as both a determinant and an outcome of tourism flows. Yet empirical evidence on whether and how ESG factors are associated with international tourist demand remains thin, fragmented, and methodologically uneven. The literature offers a mixture of cross-country regressions, case studies, and composite-score approaches, and conclusions vary substantially depending on which ESG dimensions are emphasised, how they are aggregated, and which countries are included.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Literature gap paragraph (co-authors to populate)

Three points to establish. First, prior work tends to use either composite ESG scores that mask within-pillar heterogeneity or single-indicator analyses that miss the joint structure of ESG. Second, European panel evidence is limited and rarely tested for fragility across specification choices. Third, the heterogeneity between transition and frontier European economies is undertheorised in the tourism context.
:::

This paper studies how disaggregated ESG factors are associated with international tourist arrivals in a panel of 27 European countries observed annually over 2000 to 2023. We address three questions. First, which environmental, social, and governance factors are robustly associated with international arrivals once country and year fixed effects absorb time-invariant country traits and common annual shocks? Second, are these associations heterogeneous between transition and frontier European economies, and through which dimensions specifically? Third, how sensitive are these conclusions to specification choices, identification framework (within-country deviations versus long-run cointegrating relationships), and the treatment of cross-sectional dependence?

Our contribution is twofold. Substantively, we document (i) a long-run co-movement between governance reform (corruption control) and international arrivals identified off persistent country reform trajectories — a relationship that does *not* survive the inclusion of country-specific linear time trends and is therefore best read as a slow-moving institutional-trajectory result rather than a within-country structural deviation result; (ii) within-country associations between air quality (PM2.5 exposure), digital infrastructure (internet penetration), unemployment, and international arrivals; and (iii) substitution-style cross-sectional dependence in residuals after year fixed effects, suggesting that improvements in any one destination partly draw demand from competing European destinations. Methodologically, we show that the within-country versus long-run identification distinction matters quantitatively for tourism-ESG analysis, that conclusions depend on how the within-pillar redundancy in governance indicators is handled, and that pooled cross-sectional learners (PCA composites, elastic net, random forest) and within-country causal estimators answer different questions and accordingly point to different ESG dimensions.

The within-pillar redundancy we document for the WGI governance indicators in European panel data may apply more broadly to ESG measurement systems with similar internal structure. We do not claim, and the present analysis cannot establish, that this generalises beyond our setting; future work could test the redundancy structure in other ESG measurement contexts.

The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant literature. Section 3 develops the theoretical framework and hypotheses. Section 4 describes the panel data and the cleaning pipeline. Section 5 sets out the empirical strategy and the diagnostic battery. Section 6 presents the results, including the new long-run, cross-sectional-dependence-robust, and imputation-uncertainty-propagating estimators. Section 7 discusses interpretation, mechanisms, and limitations. Section 8 concludes.

## Governance, institutional quality, and international tourism {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
Cover prior empirical work linking corruption, rule of law, political stability, and government effectiveness to tourism flows. Note the heavy reliance on cross-country regressions, the relative shortage of within-country panel evidence, and within that literature the convention of using **control of corruption** rather than rule of law as the headline governance proxy in tourism applications. Cite specific tourism papers using corruption (Poprawe 2015; Saha and Yap 2014; Yap and Saha 2013; Das and DiRienzo 2010) so that the choice in our Section 4.5 has a literature anchor.
:::

## Environmental conditions and destination choice {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
Cover air quality, climate, biodiversity, and pollution as correlates of destination demand. Note the emerging literature on PM2.5 and tourism, the simultaneity / reverse-causality issue (tourist activity also generates emissions), and the gap regarding within-country identification.
:::

## Digital infrastructure and tourism mobility {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
Cover the role of internet penetration, digital booking platforms, and information frictions in international travel. Note the saturation hypothesis for frontier economies and the granger-causality evidence (one-way precedence) that supports a stronger interpretation here than for the other regressors.
:::

## ESG measurement, composite indices versus disaggregated indicators {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
Cover the methodological literature on ESG aggregation, the disagreement among rating providers, and the critique of composite scores. Position our theory-sparse approach against this background, and note that we do *not* claim our theory-sparse versus kitchen-sink contrast generalises beyond the WGI governance pillar in European panel data.
:::

## European tourism in panel: prior evidence and methodological precedents {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
Cover prior panel studies of European tourism demand, with attention to specifications, identification strategies, treatment of cross-sectional dependence, and findings.
:::

# Theoretical Framework and Hypotheses

International tourism demand responds to a constellation of destination characteristics that potential travellers either observe directly or infer from country-level signals. We organise these characteristics through the ESG taxonomy because that taxonomy increasingly structures the policy and information environment in which destination choices are made.

Three transmission channels link ESG factors to international arrivals. First, *reputation*. Visible governance failures, environmental degradation, or social distress shape destination perception in source markets. Second, *supply quality*. Better governance, cleaner environments, and stronger digital infrastructure raise the underlying quality of the tourism product. Third, *institutional friction*. Stable governance and developed digital infrastructure lower the transaction costs of international travel.

Five hypotheses follow. They differ in their identifying variation, and the differentiation matters quantitatively for what the data can support.

**H1 (long-run trend co-movement).** Governance quality, measured through corruption control, is positively associated with international arrivals along persistent within-country reform trajectories over 2000-2023. *Mechanism.* Sustained improvements in corruption control build destination reputation, lower friction in tourism services, and signal credible institutional reform to source markets and travel intermediaries. *Identifying variation.* H1 is identified off the long-run trajectory of corruption control within country, not off year-on-year deviations from that trajectory. The country-specific time-trends robustness in Section 6.7 (Table 18) confirms this: once persistent country reform trajectories are absorbed, residual year-on-year deviations in corruption control display the *opposite* sign. H1 should therefore be read as a slow-moving institutional-trajectory result, not as a contemporaneous within-country deviation result.

**H2.** Air quality, captured through inverse PM2.5 exposure, is positively associated with international arrivals within country. *Mechanism.* Lower PM2.5 raises perceived destination quality and reduces health concerns. *Identifying variation.* The bidirectional Granger evidence (Appendix B) indicates a simultaneous-feedback structure; the contemporaneous coefficient mixes the structural channel with the reverse channel where tourist activity itself influences pollution. We interpret it as a co-movement, not a structural elasticity.

**H3.** Digital infrastructure, measured through internet penetration, is positively associated with international arrivals within country. *Mechanism.* Higher internet penetration lowers planning, booking, and on-site coordination costs. *Identifying variation.* The clean unidirectional Granger precedence (Appendix B) supports a within-country conditional-association reading with stronger temporal grounding than the other regressors.

**H4.** Labour market conditions, captured through inverse unemployment, are positively associated with international arrivals within country. *Mechanism.* Lower unemployment correlates with service quality, infrastructure investment, and macroeconomic stability that travellers infer through destination signals. *Identifying variation.* Failed Granger in both directions (Appendix B); we treat the coefficient as a within-country conditional association without imposing temporal ordering.

**H5.** The associations in H1 through H4 are systematically larger in transition (lower-income) European economies than in frontier (higher-income) economies, with internet penetration in frontier economies expected to display saturation. *Mechanism.* Transition economies sit further from the institutional, environmental, and digital frontier and have higher marginal scope for improvement. *Identifying variation caveat.* The saturation interpretation is conditional on within-country identifying variation in the high-income bin being comparable to the low/middle bin. Where the within-country standard-deviation ratio (low/high) exceeds 1.5 (Table 22), the saturation reading is observationally indistinguishable from reduced identifying variation, and the data cannot separate the two.

## Sample

The panel covers `r n_countries` European countries observed annually from `r year_min` through `r year_max`, yielding `r n_obs_raw` country-year observations. The country roster spans European Union members and selected non-EU European economies, deliberately constructed to provide variation in economic development sufficient to support the heterogeneity tests in Section 6.4.

**Selection rule.** The panel comprises European Union member states with continuous tourism data coverage from 2000 to 2023, plus selected non-member candidate states with comparable data availability. The United Kingdom is excluded due to a structural break in coverage following 2016 (Brexit transition) that interacts with the COVID-19 period in ways that would require a separate model. EFTA states (Norway, Switzerland, Iceland) are excluded because they sit outside the EU economic-policy framework that motivates several of the ESG measurement systems we use. The European post-Soviet states (Russia, Belarus, Ukraine, Moldova) and the Western Balkan candidate states are excluded due to discontinuous data coverage and, for several of these economies, fundamental structural shocks (the 2014 sanctions regime, the 2022 invasion of Ukraine) that violate the panel's identifying assumptions. We acknowledge that the absence of the United Kingdom in particular narrows the high-income subsample and may attenuate the H5 magnitudes; reproducing the analysis with a UK sub-panel is left to future work.

The lower-income or transition subsample comprises the European economies with mean GDP per capita over the period below the cross-country median, including the post-socialist accession states alongside the southern European economies that emerged from the late twentieth century convergence process. Five borderline countries sit close to the median and warrant sensitivity analysis (Section 5.4). The full classification with mean GDP per capita is reported in Appendix Table A1.

## Outcome variables

The primary outcome variable is the natural logarithm of international tourist arrivals. The panel contains no zero-arrivals observations (minimum value confirmed at data validation). Three additional outcome variables provide robustness across alternative scalings: log overnight stays, log arrivals per capita, and log overnight stays per square kilometre. All four outcomes are estimated in Section 6.2.

## Predictor variables

The candidate predictor universe consists of 74 ESG indicators drawn from the World Bank World Development Indicators, Eurostat, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, and the Worldwide Governance Indicators. The indicators decompose into three pillars: environmental (8 indicators), social (45 indicators), and governance (21 indicators). Of the 8 environmental indicators in the raw data (codes E1 through E9 with E1 absent due to source coverage), three are dropped at the data construction stage: E1 (no rows in source), E2 and E5 (incompatible measurement scale or coverage gaps that the four-pass cascade imputation could not bridge). Six environmental indicators (E3, E4, E6, E7, E8, E9) survive into the cleaning pipeline and are subject to the same greater-than-60-percent-missing rule as the social and governance indicators.

After preliminary screening (Section 4.5), the analysis identifies a theory-driven sparse specification consisting of five regressors that anchors the main results. Table 1 reports the definitions and sources of these five variables. GDP per capita is rescaled to units of USD 10,000 for coefficient interpretability.

```{r tbl-theory-vars}
#| label: tbl-theory-vars

tibble::tribble(
  ~Variable,             ~Definition,                                                        ~Source,
  "gov_corruption",      "Control of corruption (WGI percentile rank, 0-100)",                "Worldwide Governance Indicators",
  "env_pm25_exp",        "Population-weighted PM2.5 exposure (μg per m³)",                    "World Bank World Development Indicators",
  "soc_internet_users",  "Individuals using the internet (% of population)",                  "World Bank World Development Indicators",
  "soc_unempl_ilo",      "Unemployment, total (% of total labour force, ILO modelled)",       "International Labour Organization",
  "gov_gdp_capita",      "GDP per capita (current USD ÷ 10,000), control variable",           "World Bank World Development Indicators"
) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 1. Theory-sparse specification, variable definitions and sources. Note: gov_corruption is the WGI percentile rank (0-100).")
```

Table 1 fixes the five-regressor theory-sparse specification used throughout Section 6: `gov_corruption` for H1, `env_pm25_exp` for H2, `soc_internet_users` for H3, `soc_unempl_ilo` for H4, and `gov_gdp_capita` as a development control. The motivation for this five-variable choice — rather than the 15-variable governance pillar or the full 74-indicator universe — is the within-pillar redundancy argument developed in Section 4.5 and demonstrated empirically in Tables 11-13. Reading these definitions before Section 6 keeps the unit conventions (WGI percentile rank, μg/m³, percent, USD 10,000) tied to the magnitudes that appear in Table 3.

## Cleaning and imputation pipeline

The cleaning pipeline executes seven steps. The first renames each indicator with a pillar prefix and short mnemonic. The second verifies country, year, and observation counts. The third drops variables with more than 60 percent missing values and zero-variance variables. The fourth imputes the remaining missing values through a four-pass cascade: (i) linear interpolation within country (gaps ≤ 3 years), (ii) edge fill within country (cap 2 years), (iii) year-specific median across countries, (iv) global median fallback. The fifth winsorizes every ESG variable at the 1st and 99th percentiles. The sixth constructs the four derived outcome variables. The seventh validates the cleaned dataset.

The implementation tracks imputation provenance per cell. This provenance system underwrites the per-variable imputation rate diagnostic, the strict-subsample rerun in Section 6.7, and the multiple-imputation-with-Rubin's-rules robustness in Section 6.12.

**Winsorization choice.** The 1st/99th percentile cutoff follows convention in panel data work with heavy-tailed regressors and balances tail-robustness against information loss; alternative cutoffs (5th/95th, no winsorization) are tested in Table 17 and yield negligible differences. The Table 17 unwinsorized result confirms that the headline coefficients are not driven by tail observations.

Two limitations of the cleaning pipeline merit explicit acknowledgement. First, year-median imputation imports cross-country variation into observations that originally had within-country gaps. Second, winsorization compresses extreme values. Section 6.7 reports a strict-subsample rerun excluding year-median and global-median imputed observations on the headline regressors, and Section 6.12 reports a multiple-imputation analysis that *propagates* imputation uncertainty into standard errors via Rubin's rules.

```{r drop-and-impute}
#| label: drop-and-impute
#| include: false

missing_pct <- dta %>%
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric), ~ mean(is.na(.)) * 100)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "pct_miss")
high_missing <- missing_pct %>% filter(pct_miss > 60) %>% pull(var)
if (length(high_missing) > 0) dta <- select(dta, -all_of(high_missing))
zero_var <- dta %>%
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ var(., na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "v") %>%
  filter(is.na(v) | v < 1e-10) %>%
  pull(var)
if (length(zero_var) > 0) dta <- select(dta, -all_of(zero_var))

esg_vars <- dta %>%
  select(starts_with("env_"), starts_with("gov_"), starts_with("soc_")) %>%
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>%
  names()

# Snapshot raw (pre-imputation) values for the multiple-imputation analysis
dta_pre_imp <- dta

prov <- matrix("missing", nrow = nrow(dta), ncol = length(esg_vars),
               dimnames = list(NULL, esg_vars))
for (v in esg_vars) prov[!is.na(dta[[v]]), v] <- "original"

dta <- dta %>%
  group_by(Country) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(esg_vars),
                ~ zoo::na.approx(., x = Year, na.rm = FALSE, maxgap = 3))) %>%
  ungroup()
for (v in esg_vars) {
  newly_filled <- prov[, v] == "missing" & !is.na(dta[[v]])
  prov[newly_filled, v] <- "linear_interp"
}

edge_fill_within <- function(x, max_run = 2) {
  n <- length(x)
  if (n == 0 || all(is.na(x))) return(x)
  nonna <- which(!is.na(x))
  first_idx <- nonna[1]
  last_idx  <- nonna[length(nonna)]
  if (first_idx > 1) {
    k <- min(first_idx - 1, max_run)
    x[(first_idx - k):(first_idx - 1)] <- x[first_idx]
  }
  if (last_idx < n) {
    k <- min(n - last_idx, max_run)
    x[(last_idx + 1):(last_idx + k)] <- x[last_idx]
  }
  x
}
dta <- dta %>%
  group_by(Country) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(esg_vars), edge_fill_within)) %>%
  ungroup()
for (v in esg_vars) {
  newly_filled <- prov[, v] == "missing" & !is.na(dta[[v]])
  prov[newly_filled, v] <- "edge_fill"
}

dta <- dta %>%
  group_by(Year) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(esg_vars),
                ~ ifelse(is.na(.), median(., na.rm = TRUE), .))) %>%
  ungroup()
for (v in esg_vars) {
  newly_filled <- prov[, v] == "missing" & !is.na(dta[[v]])
  prov[newly_filled, v] <- "year_median"
}

dta <- dta %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(esg_vars),
                ~ ifelse(is.na(.), median(., na.rm = TRUE), .)))
for (v in esg_vars) {
  newly_filled <- prov[, v] == "missing" & !is.na(dta[[v]])
  prov[newly_filled, v] <- "global_median"
}

dta_clean <- dta
provenance_long <- as_tibble(prov) %>%
  mutate(Country = dta_clean$Country, Year = dta_clean$Year) %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(Country, Year), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Source")

n_dropped_sparse <- length(high_missing)
n_dropped_zerovar <- length(zero_var)
```

```{r winsorize-and-derive}
#| label: winsorize-and-derive
#| include: false

dta_unwinsorized <- dta_clean

dta_clean <- dta_clean %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(esg_vars), ~ {
    lo <- quantile(., 0.01, na.rm = TRUE); hi <- quantile(., 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)
    pmax(pmin(., hi), lo)
  }))

stopifnot(min(dta_clean$tour_arrivals, na.rm = TRUE) > 0)

build_outcomes <- function(d) {
  d %>%
    mutate(
      log_arrivals    = log(tour_arrivals),
      log_nights      = if ("tour_nights"        %in% names(.)) log(tour_nights)        else NA_real_,
      log_arrival_pop = if ("tour_arrival_pop"   %in% names(.)) log(tour_arrival_pop)   else NA_real_,
      log_night_area  = if ("tour_night_density" %in% names(.)) log(tour_night_density) else NA_real_
    )
}
dta_clean        <- build_outcomes(dta_clean)
dta_unwinsorized <- build_outcomes(dta_unwinsorized)

if ("gov_gdp_capita" %in% names(dta_clean)) {
  country_gdp <- dta_clean %>%
    group_by(Country) %>%
    summarise(avg_gdp = mean(gov_gdp_capita, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(high_income = as.integer(avg_gdp > median(avg_gdp, na.rm = TRUE)))
  dta_clean        <- dta_clean        %>% left_join(country_gdp %>% select(Country, high_income), by = "Country")
  dta_unwinsorized <- dta_unwinsorized %>% left_join(country_gdp %>% select(Country, high_income), by = "Country")
}

n_high   <- length(unique(dta_clean$Country[dta_clean$high_income == 1]))
n_low    <- length(unique(dta_clean$Country[dta_clean$high_income == 0]))
n_obs_hi <- sum(dta_clean$high_income == 1)
n_obs_lo <- sum(dta_clean$high_income == 0)
gdp_threshold <- median(country_gdp$avg_gdp, na.rm = TRUE)

dta_clean        <- dta_clean        %>% mutate(gov_gdp_capita = gov_gdp_capita / 10000)
dta_unwinsorized <- dta_unwinsorized %>% mutate(gov_gdp_capita = gov_gdp_capita / 10000)

dta_clean$year_num <- as.numeric(as.character(dta_clean$Year))

pdata <- pdata.frame(dta_clean, index = c("Country", "Year"), drop.index = FALSE)
```

The cleaning pipeline drops `r n_dropped_sparse` variables for excessive missingness and `r n_dropped_zerovar` for zero variance. The remaining `r length(esg_vars)` ESG variables provide the analytic universe. The retained panel of `r nrow(dta_clean)` country-year observations exhibits no residual missingness on these variables.

## Variable selection

The choice of `gov_corruption` as the governance proxy is anchored by tourism theory and confirmed by multicollinearity diagnostics. The tourism-corruption literature (Poprawe 2015; Saha and Yap 2014; Yap and Saha 2013; Das and DiRienzo 2010) consistently uses *control of corruption* rather than *rule of law* as the governance proxy of choice in international-arrivals models, because corruption is the governance dimension most directly linked to the destination-quality reputation channel: visitor harassment, petty bribery at borders and police checkpoints, and integrity in tourist services are the channels through which institutional quality affects the visitor experience. Rule of law is a broader construct that captures contract enforcement, property rights, and judicial independence — relevant primarily for inbound investment rather than for the visitor experience.

The multicollinearity diagnostic *confirms* the theoretical choice. Within-country variance inflation factors and pairwise within-country correlations among the four governance pillar variables (`gov_corruption`, `gov_effectiveness`, `gov_pol_stability`, `gov_rule_law`) reveal that `gov_rule_law` and `gov_corruption` share approximately 62 percent of their within-country variance (Section 6.6). Including both in the same regression allocates the institutional-quality effect to whichever variable enters first. The theoretically-motivated retention of `gov_corruption` therefore aligns with the multicollinearity evidence rather than being driven by it.

Hypotheses H2-H4 nominate the remaining three regressors directly (PM2.5, internet penetration, unemployment), and GDP per capita enters as a development control. The cross-method comparison in Section 6.5 places the theory-sparse specification alongside PCA composites, elastic net, and random forest, which document the divergence between cross-sectional and within-country importance — itself an informative finding rather than a competition the theory-sparse specification needs to win.

## Income classification

Following the procedure described in Section 4.1, countries are partitioned by mean GDP per capita over 2000-2023 at the median value of `r format(round(gdp_threshold, 0), big.mark = ",")` US dollars. The higher-income subsample contains `r n_high` countries and `r n_obs_hi` observations. The lower-income or transition subsample contains `r n_low` countries and `r n_obs_lo` observations. Five borderline countries (Czech Republic, Slovenia, Slovakia, Greece, Portugal) sit close to the threshold; sensitivity to their classification is assessed in Section 5.4 (Table 21) and to the classification baseline year in Table 23.

## Descriptive statistics

Table 2 reports descriptive statistics for the four outcome variables and the five theory-sparse regressors over the full sample. GDP per capita is reported in USD 10,000 units. `gov_corruption` ranges from approximately 45 to 100 on the WGI percentile-rank scale, consistent with Table 1.

```{r tbl-descriptives}
#| label: tbl-descriptives

theory_vars <- c("gov_corruption", "env_pm25_exp", "soc_internet_users",
                 "soc_unempl_ilo", "gov_gdp_capita")
outcome_vars <- c("log_arrivals", "log_nights", "log_arrival_pop", "log_night_area")

outcome_labels <- c(
  log_arrivals    = "Tourist arrivals (log)",
  log_nights      = "Tourist nights (log)",
  log_arrival_pop = "Tourist arrivals divided by population (log)",
  log_night_area  = "Tourist nights divided by area (log)"
)

desc_one <- function(data, vars) {
  data %>%
    select(all_of(vars)) %>%
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "v") %>%
    group_by(Variable) %>%
    summarise(
      N    = sum(!is.na(v)),
      Mean = round(mean(v, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      SD   = round(sd(v,   na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      Min  = round(min(v,  na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      Max  = round(max(v,  na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

bind_rows(
  desc_one(dta_clean, outcome_vars) %>%
    mutate(Group = "Outcomes",
           Variable = unname(outcome_labels[Variable])),
  desc_one(dta_clean, theory_vars)  %>%
    mutate(Group = "Theory-sparse regressors")
) %>%
  arrange(Group, Variable) %>%
  select(Group, Variable, N, Mean, SD, Min, Max) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 2. Descriptive statistics, full sample. gov_gdp_capita in USD 10,000 units; gov_corruption is the WGI percentile rank (0-100).")
```

Table 2 documents the cross-country range over which the panel identifies. The four outcomes vary by orders of magnitude across countries (Mediterranean and Alpine destinations sit at the top of the arrivals distribution, smaller Central and Eastern European economies at the bottom), while `gov_corruption` ranges over roughly 45-100 percentile-rank points and `soc_internet_users` over the full 0-100 range across the 24 years. ESG variables are winsorised at the 1st and 99th percentiles before estimation; outcomes and identifiers are not. The cross-country dispersion shown here is partly absorbed by the country fixed effects in Section 6 — what remains is within-country variation, whose magnitude by income bin is reported in Table 22 and used as the H5 power diagnostic.

# Empirical Strategy

## Specification

The preferred specification is a two-way fixed effects panel model

$$
\log(\text{arrivals}_{it}) = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \beta_1 \text{corruption}_{it} + \beta_2 \text{PM2.5}_{it} + \beta_3 \text{internet}_{it} + \beta_4 \text{unemployment}_{it} + \beta_5 \text{GDP per capita}_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
$$

The country fixed effects $\alpha_i$ absorb time-invariant country characteristics. The year fixed effects $\lambda_t$ absorb common annual shocks. The remaining beta coefficients identify within-country partial correlations conditional on the absorbed heterogeneity. The specification is estimated separately on each of the four outcome variables.

## Identification

Identification rests on three assumptions: (i) conditional on controls and after absorbing country and year fixed effects, the remaining within-country variation is exogenous to country-specific tourism shocks; (ii) slow-moving institutional and infrastructure variables exhibit sufficient within-country variation across the 24-year panel; (iii) contemporaneous specifications adequately capture the relevant adjustment horizon.

**Granger evidence and regressor-specific identification framing.** Appendix Table A2 reports pairwise Granger causality tests. `soc_internet_users` shows clean unidirectional Granger precedence (forward p < 0.0001, reverse p ≈ 0.16) and can carry stronger associational language conditional on temporal precedence. `gov_corruption` and `soc_unempl_ilo` fail Granger in both directions; for these two regressors we use *within-country conditional association* language and the coefficients should not be read as one-way structural pathways. `env_pm25_exp` shows bidirectional Granger precedence — the contemporaneous coefficient mixes the structural channel with the reverse channel and must be interpreted with corresponding caution.

**Long-run versus short-run distinction.** Slow-moving institutional and infrastructure regressors after country fixed effects capture short-run deviations from a country's long-run trajectory. The interpretive language across Sections 6 and 7 is calibrated to this distinction, and Sections 6.8-6.9 estimate explicitly long-run cointegrating relationships and Pooled Mean Group / Mean Group dynamics that decompose the data into long-run equilibrium and short-run error correction.

**Critical caveat for H1 (gov_corruption).** Once country-specific linear time trends are added (Section 6.7, Table 18), the coefficient on `gov_corruption` flips sign and becomes negatively significant. This means the H1 association documented in Table 3 is identified off the *long-run trajectory* of corruption control within each country (the slow upward reform path that runs in parallel with the long-run upward path of tourism), not off year-on-year deviations from that trajectory. We accept the country-trends evidence and frame H1 explicitly as a long-run trend co-movement result throughout the paper. The substantive interpretation is that corruption reform is a process that unfolds slowly alongside tourism development, and the contemporaneous within-country deviation is a poor proxy for the institutional-quality channel H1 actually proposes. The PMG and CCE estimators in Sections 6.9-6.10 provide the formal long-run-equilibrium machinery that this reframe requires.

Three identification concerns deserve explicit acknowledgement. First, reverse causality, since tourism revenue funds public goods, governance reforms, and infrastructure investment. Second, the slow-moving nature of governance and infrastructure regressors. Third, imputation contamination from year-median imputation. The diagnostic battery and robustness panels (Sections 6.7-6.15) address each of these.

## Estimation and inference

All models are estimated by ordinary least squares with two-way fixed effects, implemented in R using `plm` and `fixest`. Inference proceeds through three layers, ordered by which is primary given the cross-sectional dependence evidence below.

```{r diag-pesaran-cd}
#| label: diag-pesaran-cd
#| include: false
theory_rhs_prelim <- paste(c("gov_corruption", "env_pm25_exp", "soc_internet_users",
                              "soc_unempl_ilo", "gov_gdp_capita"), collapse = " + ")
m_plm_cd <- tryCatch(
  plm(as.formula(paste("log_arrivals ~", theory_rhs_prelim)),
      data = pdata, model = "within", effect = "twoways",
      index = c("Country", "Year")),
  error = function(e) NULL
)
cd_result <- if (!is.null(m_plm_cd)) tryCatch(pcdtest(m_plm_cd, test = "cd"), error = function(e) NULL) else NULL
cd_stat <- if (!is.null(cd_result)) round(cd_result$statistic, 3) else NA_real_
cd_p    <- if (!is.null(cd_result)) fmt_p(cd_result$p.value) else NA_character_
```

The Pesaran (2004) CD statistic on Table 3 residuals is `r cd_stat` (p = `r cd_p`). The CD statistic is asymptotically standard normal under the null of no cross-sectional dependence and is constructed as a normalised average of pairwise residual correlations. A *negative* CD value indicates that the average pairwise residual correlation across countries is negative — unusual for European macro panels, where common shocks (financial crisis, sovereign debt crisis, COVID-19) typically generate *positive* dependence. We interpret the negative CD value as evidence of substitution dynamics in European tourism flows: after year fixed effects absorb the global shock component, a country gaining tourists tends to coincide with neighbouring or competing countries losing tourists. This is substantively interesting (and we return to it in the discussion) but it also means that country-level cluster-robust standard errors are not the appropriate primary inference here: cluster-robust SEs at the country level allow within-country temporal dependence but do not allow across-country contemporaneous dependence.

We therefore reorganise inference as follows. **Driscoll-Kraay (1998) standard errors** are the primary inference; they are robust to cross-sectional dependence and to within-country temporal autocorrelation up to a chosen lag. The maxlag parameter is selected via the Newey-West rule applied to the time dimension T=24. **Country cluster-robust** standard errors are reported as a secondary inference benchmark for comparability with the prior literature. **Wild cluster bootstrap** p-values (Webb 6-point weights, B = 9,999) are reported as a small-sample inference check given the 27-cluster panel (Cameron, Gelbach, Miller 2008; MacKinnon and Webb 2018). The Webb 6-point distribution is the documented best practice for small G. Section 6.10 also reports a **Common Correlated Effects Mean Group (CCEMG)** estimator (Pesaran 2006; Chudik and Pesaran 2015) that handles cross-sectional dependence inside the slope estimation, not only in the standard errors.

**Heterogeneous slopes and the continuous-treatment TWFE bias literature.** With five continuous regressors and country plus year fixed effects, the pooled-slope TWFE coefficients in Table 3 are weighted averages over heterogeneous within-country relationships. de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2020, 2024) show that with continuous treatments and TWFE the implicit weights can be negative for some country-year cells and the pooled coefficient does not in general coincide with a simple average of unit-time treatment effects. We address this exposure by reporting the Mean Group estimator in Section 6.9 (Table 26) as the heterogeneous-slope robustness check; if the MG long-run coefficient and the TWFE coefficient agree in sign and rough magnitude, the negative-weighting concern is empirically discharged for the regressor in question. Where they diverge, the divergence is itself a result and is interpreted in the discussion.

**Year fixed effects and the global ESG common factor.** The main TWFE specification absorbs year fixed effects, which removes anything that moves common across countries in a given year. This includes the global trend in internet adoption, the global decline in PM2.5, and the global trend in governance scores. The H2-H4 coefficients are therefore identified off within-country deviations from these global trends, not off the global trends themselves. This is a deliberate identifying restriction (it absorbs simultaneous global confounders) but it changes the question the coefficients answer: not "does internet adoption raise tourism" but "does within-country internet adoption deviation from the global trend raise tourism". The CCEMG estimator in Section 6.10 (Table 27) provides the alternative reading by replacing year fixed effects with cross-sectional means of the dependent variable and regressors as proxies for the unobserved common factor structure; this allows more of the common variation back into the slope estimation. We treat TWFE and CCEMG as two readings of the same data, not as a primary and a sensitivity, and we surface coefficient comparisons across the two in the discussion.

Specification choice between fixed effects and random effects is addressed by a Mundlak test (Appendix D). With p ≈ 0.110 the test does not reject the random-effects null at conventional levels. We retain fixed effects on substantive grounds: (i) the Mundlak test has limited power in a panel with N = 27 and slow-moving regressors with low within-country variance, so failure to reject is weak evidence; (ii) the *levels* of corruption control, internet penetration, and PM2.5 exposure are likely correlated with permanent country unobservables (cultural orientation, geographic position relative to source markets, established tourism infrastructure) that also affect tourism, and random-effects estimation that weights between-country variation imports this correlation into the estimated coefficients. The correlated random effects (Mundlak hybrid; Wooldridge 2010) specification in Section 6.11 (Table 28) reports the within-between decomposition explicitly and is read as a complement to TWFE rather than as a sensitivity check.

## Heterogeneity analysis

To test H5, the panel is partitioned by mean GDP per capita as described in Section 4.7, and the theory-sparse specification is estimated separately on each subsample. Coefficients on `gov_corruption`, `env_pm25_exp`, and `soc_internet_users` are compared across bins. The stratified estimation is supplemented by a formal interaction specification with a joint Wald test of all four interaction terms (Table 7). Sensitivity to classification is assessed by relabelling the five borderline countries one at a time (Table 21), by alternative 2000 and 2023 baseline classifications (Table 23), and by surfacing the within-country SD ratios by income bin (Table 22). Where the within-country SD ratio (low/high) exceeds 1.5 for the regressor that drives an H5 contrast, we explicitly retreat from the saturation reading and substitute "consistent with both saturation and reduced identifying variation; the data cannot distinguish."

## Robustness battery

The robustness battery comprises panels reported in Sections 6.2 through 6.15. The descriptive sensitivity set (outcome variation, COVID period, imputation provenance, winsorization, kitchen-sink, country trends, quadratic saturation, leave-one-country-out, borderline reclassification, within-country SD diagnostic, income classification, lagged regressors) is supplemented by: (a) panel cointegration tests, (b) Pooled Mean Group / Mean Group estimators, (c) Common Correlated Effects estimators, (d) correlated random effects (Mundlak hybrid), (e) multiple imputation with Rubin's rules, (f) specification curve, (g) held-out 2000-2011 / 2012-2023 validation, and (h) a first-differenced specification contingent on the cointegration result.

## Multiple-testing declaration and pre-registration disclosure

The four primary inferences of the paper are the four headline coefficients in Table 3, one per H1-H4. Holm-corrected p-values across these four tests are reported alongside the raw p-values in Table 3. Tables 4-24 are positioned as descriptive sensitivity analyses, not as independent significance tests; we drop significance asterisks from the sensitivity tables where the focus is coefficient stability rather than null rejection.

**Pre-registration status.** The five hypotheses H1-H5 were pre-stated at the start of this project and have remained unchanged. Specifications evolved during the empirical work in response to robustness diagnostics, in particular the country-trends test that motivated the H1 reframe and the cross-sectional dependence evidence that motivated the inference reorganisation. The four primary tests as the Holm correction family is logically derivable from the pre-stated hypotheses (H5 is a heterogeneity hypothesis tested via subsample interactions, leaving H1 to H4 as the four headline coefficients) but the family was specified after substantial specification work and is therefore an ex-post selection. The Holm correction controls family-wise error rate within the four pre-stated hypotheses but does not substitute for specification pre-registration. The held-out validation in Section 6.14 functions as a partial pre-registration substitute.

## Diagnostic battery

The diagnostic battery comprises within R-squared by candidate regressor after FE absorption, per-variable imputation rates, within-country distinct-value counts, within-demeaned VIFs and pairwise correlations among the governance pillar variables, country-blocked CV R-squared for the random forest (now compared apples-to-apples to the TWFE within-R² from the same five features), and the Pesaran CD test reported above.

# Results

## Methodological choices

For procedural transparency we list the parametric choices made in the estimation pipeline. **Driscoll-Kraay maxlag.** Selected via the Newey-West rule applied to the time dimension T=24, giving maxlag=3. **CCE pooling decision.** CCEMG (heterogeneous slopes Mean Group variant) is reported in Table 27. CCEP (pooled) is not reported because heterogeneous slopes is the relevant null under the de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2024) considerations. **PMG vs MG.** Both are reported in Table 26. The Hausman test of long-run homogeneity discriminates: rejection favours MG (heterogeneous long-run slopes); failure to reject favours PMG (more efficient under homogeneity). **Multiple imputation.** mice with method="pmm" (predictive mean matching), m=20 imputations, seed=42, default mice predictor matrix (all other variables in the dataset, including the dependent variable). Pooling uses Barnard and Rubin (1999) small-sample df. **Specification curve grid.** 96 specifications across governance proxy (3) × outcome (4) × COVID inclusion (2) × country trends (2) × winsorization (2). The grid was constructed ex post and is presented as a robustness diagnostic, not a confirmatory test. **Cointegration tests.** Maddala-Wu (1999) Fisher pooling reported as a per-country diagnostic; Westerlund (2007) Gt and Ga group-mean ECM-based statistics reported as the formal cointegration test under cross-sectional dependence. **Wild cluster bootstrap.** Webb 6-point distribution per MacKinnon and Webb (2018), B=9,999.

```{r helper-fe}
#| label: helper-fe
#| include: false

run_fe2 <- function(formula_str, data) {
  m <- plm(as.formula(formula_str), data = data, model = "within", effect = "twoways",
           index = c("Country", "Year"))
  vc <- vcovHC(m, type = "HC1", cluster = "group")
  list(model = m, ct = coeftest(m, vcov = vc),
       within_r2 = unname(summary(m)$r.squared[1]),
       n = nobs(m))
}

# Driscoll-Kraay coeftest for a plm object (maxlag uses time dimension T, not nobs)
run_fe2_dk <- function(formula_str, data, maxlag = NULL) {
  m <- plm(as.formula(formula_str), data = data, model = "within", effect = "twoways",
           index = c("Country", "Year"))
  if (is.null(maxlag)) {
    T_dim <- length(unique(as.numeric(as.character(index(m, "time")))))
    maxlag <- floor(4 * (T_dim / 100)^(2/9))
  }
  vc_dk <- tryCatch(vcovSCC(m, type = "HC1", maxlag = maxlag),
                    error = function(e) vcovHC(m, type = "HC1", cluster = "group"))
  list(model = m, ct = coeftest(m, vcov = vc_dk),
       within_r2 = unname(summary(m)$r.squared[1]),
       n = nobs(m),
       dk_lag = maxlag)
}

theory_rhs <- paste(theory_vars, collapse = " + ")
```

## Main estimates

Table 3 reports the theory-sparse two-way fixed effects estimates on log arrivals over the full sample. Three p-value columns are shown: Driscoll-Kraay (primary, robust to cross-sectional dependence per the negative Pesaran CD), country cluster-robust (asymptotic), and wild cluster bootstrap (Rademacher, B = 9,999). A Holm-adjusted p-value across the four H1-H4 primary tests is reported as the final column; the Bonferroni-Holm threshold for the smallest p-value in a four-test family at α = 0.05 is 0.0125.

**Read alongside Table 18.** The H1 coefficient on `gov_corruption` reflects long-run trend co-movement; Section 6.7 documents that it does *not* survive country-specific time trends. The H2-H4 coefficients survive that test.

```{r tbl-main}
#| label: tbl-main
main_arr     <- run_fe2(paste("log_arrivals ~", theory_rhs), pdata)
main_arr_dk  <- run_fe2_dk(paste("log_arrivals ~", theory_rhs), pdata)

cap_main <- sprintf("Table 3. Theory-sparse two-way fixed effects, log arrivals (full sample, n = %d, within R-squared = %.3f, Driscoll-Kraay maxlag = %d). p_dk = Driscoll-Kraay (primary); p_clu = cluster-robust (country); p_boot = wild cluster bootstrap (Webb 6-point, B = 9,999); p_holm = Holm correction across H1-H4. Coef_std = beta times within-country SD of regressor (standardised within coefficient).",
                    main_arr$n, main_arr$within_r2, main_arr_dk$dk_lag)

m_fe_fixest <- tryCatch(
  feols(as.formula(paste("log_arrivals ~", theory_rhs, "| Country + Year")),
        data = dta_clean, cluster = ~Country),
  error = function(e) NULL
)

# Webb 6-point bootstrap distribution per MacKinnon and Webb (2018)
boot_results <- if (!is.null(m_fe_fixest)) {
  boot_vars <- c("gov_corruption", "env_pm25_exp", "soc_internet_users", "soc_unempl_ilo", "gov_gdp_capita")
  boot_vars_avail <- intersect(boot_vars, names(coef(m_fe_fixest)))
  map_dfr(boot_vars_avail, function(v) {
    br <- tryCatch(
      boottest(m_fe_fixest, param = v, clustid = "Country", B = 9999,
               type = "webb", seed = 42),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    if (is.null(br)) return(data.frame(Variable = v, p_boot = NA_character_))
    data.frame(Variable = v, p_boot = fmt_p(br$p_val))
  })
} else {
  data.frame(Variable = character(), p_boot = character())
}

# Within-country standard deviation for each theory regressor
within_sd <- dta_clean %>%
  group_by(Country) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(theory_vars), ~ . - mean(., na.rm = TRUE),
                .names = "{.col}_within")) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  summarise(across(ends_with("_within"), ~ sd(., na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "within_sd") %>%
  mutate(Variable = sub("_within$", "", Variable))

# Build columns: cluster-robust (from main_arr) and Driscoll-Kraay (from main_arr_dk)
ct_clu <- as.data.frame(unclass(main_arr$ct))    %>% rownames_to_column("Variable")
ct_dk  <- as.data.frame(unclass(main_arr_dk$ct)) %>% rownames_to_column("Variable")

tbl3 <- ct_dk %>%
  transmute(Variable,
            Coef = round(Estimate, 4),
            SE_dk = round(`Std. Error`, 4),
            p_dk  = fmt_p(`Pr(>|t|)`),
            p_dk_raw = `Pr(>|t|)`,
            Coef_raw = Estimate) %>%
  left_join(ct_clu %>% transmute(Variable,
                                 SE_clu = round(`Std. Error`, 4),
                                 p_clu  = fmt_p(`Pr(>|t|)`)),
            by = "Variable") %>%
  left_join(boot_results, by = "Variable") %>%
  left_join(within_sd, by = "Variable") %>%
  mutate(Coef_std = round(Coef_raw * within_sd, 4))

# Holm across the four primary H1-H4 tests, using the DK p-values
primary <- c("gov_corruption", "env_pm25_exp", "soc_internet_users", "soc_unempl_ilo")
holm_p <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(tbl3))
mask <- tbl3$Variable %in% primary
holm_p[mask] <- p.adjust(tbl3$p_dk_raw[mask], method = "holm")
tbl3$p_holm <- ifelse(is.na(holm_p), NA_character_, fmt_p(holm_p))
tbl3$p_dk_raw <- NULL
tbl3$Coef_raw <- NULL
tbl3$within_sd <- NULL

tbl3 %>%
  select(Variable, Coef, Coef_std, SE_dk, p_dk, SE_clu, p_clu, p_boot, p_holm) %>%
  kable(caption = cap_main)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Co-authors — substantive interpretation

Translate coefficients into substantive percentage interpretations. Note three things explicitly:

1. **gov_corruption is on the WGI percentile-rank scale (0-100), not standard-normal units.** A coefficient of β around 0.0098 means a 1-percentile-rank improvement is associated with about 0.98% more arrivals; a 10-percentile-rank improvement (typical decadal reform progress for a transition economy) corresponds to about 9.8% more arrivals. The standardised within coefficient column (Coef_std = β times within-country SD of regressor) gives the cross-coefficient comparable magnitude. Per Section 6.7 / Table 18 the H1 reading is long-run trend co-movement, not within-country structural deviation.

2. **soc_internet_users has temporal precedence (Granger) and can carry conditional-association language.** gov_corruption and soc_unempl_ilo have ambiguous temporal ordering. env_pm25_exp has bidirectional Granger and should be framed as a simultaneous feedback co-movement.

3. **Holm correction.** Identify which of H1-H4 survive at the Holm-adjusted threshold and discuss the implication.
:::

**Within R² interpretation.** The within R² of 0.299 indicates that the five theory-sparse regressors explain roughly 30 percent of within-country variation in log arrivals. The remaining 70 percent reflects source-country shocks, exchange-rate fluctuations, idiosyncratic destination-specific events (terrorism, natural disasters, sporting events), and other covariates not in the five-regressor set. The kitchen-sink specification in Section 6.5 documents the residual variance accessible to a richer regressor set. The theory-sparse specification is meant to identify partial associations on five pre-specified ESG channels, not to maximise predictive fit; the within R² is reported for transparency rather than as the primary inferential object.

## Outcome robustness

```{r tbl-outcomes}
#| label: tbl-outcomes
out_results <- map(set_names(outcome_vars), ~ run_fe2_dk(paste(.x, "~", theory_rhs), pdata))
out_table <- map_dfr(names(out_results), function(dv) {
  ct <- out_results[[dv]]$ct
  data.frame(
    DV = dv,
    Variable = rownames(ct),
    Coef = round(ct[, "Estimate"], 4),
    SE   = round(ct[, "Std. Error"], 4),
    p    = fmt_p(ct[, "Pr(>|t|)"]),
    Within_R2 = round(out_results[[dv]]$within_r2, 3),
    N = out_results[[dv]]$n
  )
})
out_table %>%
  filter(Variable %in% theory_vars) %>%
  mutate(DV = unname(outcome_labels[DV])) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 4. Theory-sparse coefficients across four outcome variables (Driscoll-Kraay SEs, maxlag=3). Coefficient stability is the focus; significance asterisks omitted to avoid implying these are independent inferences.")
```

**Outcome scaling convergence.** Across the four outcome scalings (log arrivals, log nights, log arrivals per capita, log nights per area), the H1-H4 coefficients are consistently signed and within roughly 30 percent of the headline magnitude on the log arrivals scale. The gov_corruption coefficient is positive across all four scalings; env_pm25_exp is negative across all four; soc_internet_users is positive across all four; soc_unempl_ilo is negative across all four. This sign convergence across scalings discharges the concern that the headline results are an artefact of the arrivals-specific outcome construction.

## COVID period sensitivity

```{r tbl-covid}
#| label: tbl-covid
excl_list <- list(
  "Full sample"   = integer(0),
  "Excl 2020"     = 2020L,
  "Excl 2021"     = 2021L,
  "Excl 2022"     = 2022L,
  "Excl 2020-22"  = 2020L:2022L
)
covid_fits <- lapply(excl_list, function(yrs) {
  pd <- pdata.frame(dta_clean %>% filter(!Year %in% yrs), index = c("Country", "Year"))
  run_fe2_dk(paste("log_arrivals ~", theory_rhs), pd)
})
covid_full <- covid_fits[["Full sample"]]
covid_excl <- covid_fits[["Excl 2020-22"]]

bind_rows(
  lapply(names(covid_fits), function(nm) {
    f <- covid_fits[[nm]]
    extract_coef_table(f$ct) %>%
      mutate(Sample = sprintf("%s (n=%d, R²=%.3f)", nm, f$n, f$within_r2))
  })
) %>%
  filter(Variable %in% theory_vars) %>%
  select(Sample, Variable, Coef, SE, p) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 5. COVID period sensitivity. Driscoll-Kraay SEs; sensitivity reading, asterisks omitted.")
```

Table 5 reestimates the theory-sparse specification on five COVID treatments — full sample, drop 2020, drop 2021, drop 2022, and drop the full 2020-2022 window — to confirm that the pandemic shock does not drive the headline coefficients. Across the five samples the H1-H4 coefficient signs are stable and magnitudes move within a narrow band, with the largest movement in `soc_internet_users` (consistent with the documented 2020-2021 internet-use jump). The headline conclusions on H1-H4 therefore do not hinge on the COVID disruption — they reflect within-country variation across the full 2000-2023 window rather than a 2020-2022 artefact.

## Heterogeneity

Tables 6 and 7 report the heterogeneity analysis. The differential significance pattern across income bins must be read alongside the within-country SD ratios in Table 22 (surfaced in main text below): where the low/high SD ratio exceeds 1.5, the saturation interpretation is observationally indistinguishable from reduced identifying variation in the high-income bin.

```{r tbl-het-stratified}
#| label: tbl-het-stratified
pdata_hi <- pdata.frame(dta_clean %>% filter(high_income == 1, !Year %in% 2020:2022),
                        index = c("Country", "Year"))
pdata_lo <- pdata.frame(dta_clean %>% filter(high_income == 0, !Year %in% 2020:2022),
                        index = c("Country", "Year"))
het_hi <- run_fe2_dk(paste("log_arrivals ~", theory_rhs), pdata_hi)
het_lo <- run_fe2_dk(paste("log_arrivals ~", theory_rhs), pdata_lo)
bind_rows(
  extract_coef_table(het_hi$ct) %>% mutate(Subsample = sprintf("High income (n = %d, within R^2 = %.3f)", het_hi$n, het_hi$within_r2)),
  extract_coef_table(het_lo$ct) %>% mutate(Subsample = sprintf("Low/Middle (n = %d, within R^2 = %.3f)", het_lo$n, het_lo$within_r2))
) %>%
  select(Subsample, Variable, Coef, SE, p) %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 6. Heterogeneity by income bin, theory-sparse specification on log arrivals (excluding 2020-2022, Driscoll-Kraay SEs).")
```

```{r tbl-het-interaction}
#| label: tbl-het-interaction

# Wald test. fixest names interactions like 'gov_corruption:high_income'
# (with colon) when using the * operator. We construct the model and then build the
# hypothesis vector against the actual coef names in the model.
int_fe <- tryCatch(
  feols(as.formula(paste("log_arrivals ~ gov_corruption*high_income +",
                         "env_pm25_exp*high_income + soc_internet_users*high_income +",
                         "soc_unempl_ilo*high_income + gov_gdp_capita | Country + Year")),
        data = dta_clean %>% filter(!Year %in% 2020:2022),
        cluster = ~Country),
  error = function(e) NULL
)

wald_F <- NA_real_; wald_p <- NA_character_
if (!is.null(int_fe)) {
  int_ct <- coeftest(int_fe)
  df_int <- extract_coef_table(int_ct)
  print(kable(df_int, caption = "Table 7. Interaction specification (base = low/middle income; rows containing 'high_income' report differential effects in the high-income bin)."))

  coef_names <- names(coef(int_fe))
  # find the four interaction terms by pattern match
  inter_terms <- coef_names[grepl(":high_income$|:high_income:", coef_names) |
                            grepl("^high_income:", coef_names) |
                            grepl("\\.high_income$", coef_names)]
  # Filter to the four headline regressors only
  base_inter <- c("gov_corruption", "env_pm25_exp", "soc_internet_users", "soc_unempl_ilo")
  inter_terms <- inter_terms[sapply(inter_terms, function(t) any(sapply(base_inter, function(b) grepl(b, t))))]

  if (length(inter_terms) > 0) {
    hyp <- paste0("`", inter_terms, "` = 0")
    wald_int <- tryCatch(
      car::linearHypothesis(int_fe, hyp, vcov. = vcov(int_fe, cluster = ~Country)),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    if (!is.null(wald_int)) {
      stat_col <- intersect(c("F", "Chisq"),           names(wald_int))[1]
      p_col    <- intersect(c("Pr(>F)", "Pr(>Chisq)"), names(wald_int))[1]
      wald_F <- if (!is.na(stat_col)) round(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(wald_int[[stat_col]][2])), 3) else NA_real_
      wald_p <- if (!is.na(p_col))    fmt_p(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(wald_int[[p_col]][2])))     else NA_character_
    }
  }
}
```

Joint Wald test for H5 (all four interaction terms equal zero): F = `r wald_F`, p = `r wald_p`. `r if (!is.na(wald_F)) ifelse(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(gsub("<","",wald_p))) < 0.05, "The joint test rejects homogeneity, providing evidence for differential within-country associations across income bins, conditional on the within-SD-ratio caveat in Section 5.4 / Table 22.", "The joint test does not reject homogeneity at the 5 percent level. Individual interaction terms should be interpreted with caution, particularly given the within-SD-ratio constraints documented in Table 22.") else "Wald test not estimable; see code log."`

## Cross-method comparison

Tables 8 through 10 contextualise the theory-sparse specification.

**Framing.** Elastic net (Table 9) and random forest (Table 10) are pooled cross-sectional predictors *without* fixed effects. They answer: which variables predict cross-country and cross-year *levels* of tourism? TWFE answers: which variables predict *within-country changes*. These are different questions and the evidence below shows the answers diverge — itself an informative finding rather than a competition the theory-sparse model needs to win.

```{r tbl-pca}
#| label: tbl-pca
run_pca_pc1 <- function(data, vars) {
  m <- data %>% select(all_of(vars)) %>% drop_na()
  if (ncol(m) < 2 || nrow(m) < 10) return(NULL)
  prc <- prcomp(m, scale. = TRUE, center = TRUE)
  list(prc = prc, used_rows = which(complete.cases(data[, vars])))
}
attach_pc1 <- function(data, vars, name) {
  res <- run_pca_pc1(data, vars)
  if (is.null(res)) return(data)
  data[[name]] <- NA_real_
  data[[name]][res$used_rows] <- predict(res$prc, newdata = data[res$used_rows, vars])[, 1]
  data
}
env_v <- intersect(esg_vars, names(dta_clean %>% select(starts_with("env_"))))
soc_v <- intersect(esg_vars, names(dta_clean %>% select(starts_with("soc_"))))
gov_v <- intersect(esg_vars, names(dta_clean %>% select(starts_with("gov_"))))
dta_pca <- dta_clean %>%
  attach_pc1(env_v, "env_pc1") %>%
  attach_pc1(soc_v, "soc_pc1") %>%
  attach_pc1(gov_v, "gov_pc1")
pdata_pca <- pdata.frame(dta_pca, index = c("Country", "Year"), drop.index = FALSE)
pca_fit <- run_fe2_dk("log_arrivals ~ env_pc1 + soc_pc1 + gov_pc1", pdata_pca)
extract_coef_table(pca_fit$ct) %>%
  kable(caption = sprintf("Table 8. Principal-component composites in two-way fixed effects (n = %d, within R-squared = %.3f, Driscoll-Kraay SEs).",
                          pca_fit$n, pca_fit$within_r2))
```

The insignificance of `gov_pc1` does not contradict the `gov_corruption` result. PC1 averages across governance sub-indicators that pull in different directions within country; corruption, political stability, and regulatory quality do not all move together over a 24-year panel. PC1 dilutes any single sub-indicator's signal by weighting in orthogonal noise from other dimensions. The theory-sparse retention of `gov_corruption` is anchored in the tourism-corruption literature (Section 4.5) — it is the governance sub-indicator most aligned with the tourism reputation channel, not just an opportunistically chosen statistic.

```{r tbl-en}
#| label: tbl-en
en_data <- dta_clean %>% select(log_arrivals, all_of(esg_vars)) %>% drop_na()
X <- model.matrix(log_arrivals ~ . - 1, data = en_data)
y <- en_data$log_arrivals
set.seed(42)
cv_en <- cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0.5, nfolds = 10)
en_model <- glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0.5, lambda = cv_en$lambda.1se)
en_coefs <- as.matrix(coef(en_model)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("Variable") %>%
  rename(Coef = s0) %>%
  filter(Variable != "(Intercept)", abs(Coef) > 1e-10) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(Coef))) %>%
  mutate(Coef = round(Coef, 4))
en_coefs %>% head(15) %>%
  kable(caption = sprintf("Table 9. Elastic net selection, top 15 variables (alpha = 0.5, lambda.1se = %.4f, %d total selected). Cross-sectional predictor, not a within-country causal estimator.",
                          cv_en$lambda.1se, nrow(en_coefs)))
```

```{r tbl-rf}
#| label: tbl-rf
rf_data <- dta_clean %>% select(log_arrivals, Country, all_of(esg_vars)) %>% drop_na()
set.seed(42)
rf_naive <- randomForest(
  as.formula(paste("log_arrivals ~", paste(esg_vars, collapse = " + "))),
  data = rf_data %>% select(-Country),
  ntree = 500, importance = TRUE,
  mtry = floor(sqrt(length(esg_vars)))
)
naive_r2 <- 1 - rf_naive$mse[length(rf_naive$mse)] / var(rf_data$log_arrivals)

countries_rf <- unique(rf_data$Country)
preds <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(rf_data))
for (cc in countries_rf) {
  train <- rf_data %>% filter(Country != cc) %>% select(-Country)
  test  <- rf_data %>% filter(Country == cc) %>% select(-Country)
  if (nrow(test) == 0) next
  rf_c <- randomForest(
    as.formula(paste("log_arrivals ~", paste(esg_vars, collapse = " + "))),
    data = train, ntree = 300,
    mtry = floor(sqrt(length(esg_vars)))
  )
  preds[rf_data$Country == cc] <- predict(rf_c, newdata = test)
}
ss_res <- sum((rf_data$log_arrivals - preds)^2)
ss_tot <- sum((rf_data$log_arrivals - mean(rf_data$log_arrivals))^2)
cv_r2 <- 1 - ss_res / ss_tot

# Also fit RF on the FIVE theory-sparse features only, for an apples-to-apples comparison
rf_data5 <- dta_clean %>% select(log_arrivals, Country, all_of(theory_vars)) %>% drop_na()
preds5 <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(rf_data5))
set.seed(42)
for (cc in unique(rf_data5$Country)) {
  train <- rf_data5 %>% filter(Country != cc) %>% select(-Country)
  test  <- rf_data5 %>% filter(Country == cc) %>% select(-Country)
  if (nrow(test) == 0) next
  rf_c <- randomForest(
    as.formula(paste("log_arrivals ~", paste(theory_vars, collapse = " + "))),
    data = train, ntree = 300, mtry = max(1, floor(sqrt(length(theory_vars))))
  )
  preds5[rf_data5$Country == cc] <- predict(rf_c, newdata = test)
}
ss_res5 <- sum((rf_data5$log_arrivals - preds5)^2)
ss_tot5 <- sum((rf_data5$log_arrivals - mean(rf_data5$log_arrivals))^2)
cv_r2_5feat <- 1 - ss_res5 / ss_tot5

rf_imp <- data.frame(
  Variable = rownames(importance(rf_naive)),
  IncMSE = round(importance(rf_naive)[, "%IncMSE"], 2)
) %>%
  arrange(desc(IncMSE)) %>%
  mutate(Rank = row_number(),
         Pillar = case_when(
           str_starts(Variable, "env_") ~ "Environment",
           str_starts(Variable, "soc_") ~ "Social",
           str_starts(Variable, "gov_") ~ "Governance"
         ))
rf_imp %>% head(15) %>%
  select(Rank, Variable, Pillar, IncMSE) %>%
  kable(caption = sprintf("Table 10. Random forest variable importance, top 15 (cross-sectional, pooled). Naive in-sample R² = %.3f. Country-blocked CV R² (74 features) = %.3f. Country-blocked CV R² (5 theory-sparse features only) = %.3f. TWFE within R² (5 features) = %.3f.",
                          naive_r2, cv_r2, cv_r2_5feat, main_arr$within_r2))
```

The naive in-sample R² (`r round(naive_r2, 3)`) versus country-blocked CV R² (`r round(cv_r2, 3)`) gap confirms heavy memorisation of country-level features. The apples-to-apples comparison restricts both methods to the same five theory-sparse features: random-forest country-blocked CV R² is `r round(cv_r2_5feat, 3)` and TWFE within R² is `r round(main_arr$within_r2, 3)`. The two are similar in magnitude on their respective scales (one is unconditional out-of-country prediction, the other is residual within-country variance share), and crucially the linear specification is not predictively dominated by the more flexible non-parametric alternative when both are restricted to the same feature set. This is one piece of evidence supporting the choice of two-way fixed effects with the theory-sparse feature set.

## Specification fragility

The kitchen-sink specification, which retains the full governance pillar alongside additional environmental and social controls, suppresses the corruption coefficient. Table 11 traces this through a sequential build-up of governance regressors. The corruption coefficient flips sign and loses significance at the step where `gov_rule_law` enters.

```{r tbl-buildup}
#| label: tbl-buildup
seq_specs <- list(
  c("gov_corruption"),
  c("gov_corruption", "gov_gdp_capita"),
  c("gov_corruption", "gov_gdp_capita", "gov_rule_law"),
  c("gov_corruption", "gov_gdp_capita", "gov_rule_law", "gov_effectiveness"),
  c("gov_corruption", "gov_gdp_capita", "gov_rule_law", "gov_effectiveness", "gov_pol_stability")
)
seq_results <- map_dfr(seq_along(seq_specs), function(i) {
  rhs <- paste(seq_specs[[i]], collapse = " + ")
  fit <- run_fe2_dk(paste("log_arrivals ~", rhs), pdata)
  ct  <- fit$ct
  if (!"gov_corruption" %in% rownames(ct)) return(NULL)
  data.frame(
    Step = i,
    Specification = paste(seq_specs[[i]], collapse = " + "),
    `corruption β` = round(ct["gov_corruption", "Estimate"], 4),
    SE = round(ct["gov_corruption", "Std. Error"], 4),
    p  = fmt_p(ct["gov_corruption", "Pr(>|t|)"]),
    `Within R²` = round(fit$within_r2, 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
})
seq_results %>% kable(caption = "Table 11. Sequential build-up of governance regressors. The corruption coefficient flips at Step 3 when gov_rule_law enters. (DK SEs.)")
```

The two specifications answer different conditional questions. The theory-sparse coefficient on `gov_corruption` is the partial association conditional on development and the non-governance ESG channels. The kitchen-sink coefficient is the partial association conditional on the full governance pillar — which is dominated by `gov_rule_law` because the two variables share 62% of within-country variance (Table 12). This is a within-pillar redundancy issue, not a specification-fragility issue, and we frame it accordingly. Neither coefficient is privileged a priori; the theory-sparse choice is anchored in the tourism-corruption literature (Section 4.5).

```{r tbl-correlations}
#| label: tbl-correlations
gov_pillar <- c("gov_corruption", "gov_effectiveness", "gov_rule_law",
                "gov_pol_stability", "gov_gdp_capita")
within_demean <- function(x, by) x - ave(x, by, FUN = function(v) mean(v, na.rm = TRUE))
within_df <- dta_clean %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(gov_pillar), ~ within_demean(., Country)))
within_cor <- cor(within_df[, gov_pillar], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
round(within_cor, 3) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("Variable") %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 12. Within-country pairwise correlations among governance pillar variables (after country-mean demeaning).")
```

```{r tbl-ks-comparison}

ks_vars <- c(
  "gov_corruption", "gov_effectiveness", "gov_rule_law", "gov_pol_stability", "gov_gdp_capita",
  "env_pm25_exp", "env_co2_capita", "env_renew_elec", "env_co2_gdp",
```

### Country-specific time trends — H1 caveat

Table 18 adds country-specific linear time trends. **The coefficient on `gov_corruption` flips sign and is significant at the 5% level in the negative direction.** This is the key piece of evidence behind the H1 reframe in Section 3 and Section 5.2. Once persistent country reform trajectories are absorbed, the residual year-on-year deviations in corruption control display the *opposite* sign association with arrivals. The H1 finding in Table 3 is therefore identified off long-run trend co-movement (corruption reform and tourism development both rising along persistent country-specific trajectories over 2000-2023), not off year-on-year deviations from those trajectories. We accept this evidence and frame H1 throughout the paper as a long-run-trend result. The H2-H4 coefficients hold direction under the country-trends specification and can therefore continue to be read as within-country structural deviations.

```{r tbl-ctt}
#| label: tbl-ctt
m_ctt <- tryCatch(
  feols(as.formula(paste("log_arrivals ~", theory_rhs, "| Country + Year + Country[year_num]")),
        data = dta_clean, cluster = ~Country),
  error = function(e) NULL
)
if (!is.null(m_ctt)) {
  ctt_ct <- coeftest(m_ctt)
  extract_coef_table(ctt_ct) %>%
    kable(caption = sprintf("Table 18. Country-specific linear time trends (feols, within R-squared = %.3f). Identifies within-country deviations from country-specific trends. NOTE the sign flip on gov_corruption — this is the country-trends evidence behind the H1 reframe (long-run trend co-movement, not within-country deviation).",
                            r2(m_ctt, type = "wr2")))
} else {
  kable(data.frame(Note = "Country-specific time trends model could not be estimated."),
        caption = "Table 18. Country-specific linear time trends — estimation error.")
}
```

### Oster (2019) bound for unobserved selection on H1

Reverse causality on H1 is acknowledged in Section 5.2: tourism revenue funds public goods, governance reforms, and infrastructure investment. The Oster (2019) bound quantifies how much unobserved selection on omitted country-time variables would have to operate, relative to the observed selection on the included controls, to drive the H1 coefficient to zero. Specifically, Oster's delta is the proportional selection coefficient that solves for beta=0; values of |delta| > 1 indicate that unobserved selection would have to be more important than observed selection to overturn the result.

```{r tbl-oster}
#| label: tbl-oster
# Oster (2019) bound for unobserved selection on observables on the H1 coefficient.
# Strategy: estimate uncontrolled and controlled R^2 from the same dataset and compute delta.
# We use a within-transformed dataset to keep the FE absorption consistent.

oster_result <- tryCatch({
  # Step 1: within-transform on Country and Year (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell)
  dta_w <- dta_clean %>%
    group_by(Country) %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(c("log_arrivals", theory_vars)), ~ . - mean(., na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    group_by(Year) %>%
    mutate(across(all_of(c("log_arrivals", theory_vars)), ~ . - mean(., na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
    ungroup()
  
  # Uncontrolled: gov_corruption only (after FE absorption)
  m_unc <- lm(log_arrivals ~ gov_corruption, data = dta_w)
  R2_unc <- summary(m_unc)$r.squared
  beta_unc <- coef(m_unc)["gov_corruption"]
  
  # Controlled: all theory regressors (after FE absorption)
  m_ctrl <- lm(as.formula(paste("log_arrivals ~", theory_rhs)), data = dta_w)
  R2_ctrl <- summary(m_ctrl)$r.squared
  beta_ctrl <- coef(m_ctrl)["gov_corruption"]
  
  # Oster delta solving for beta = 0 with R2max = 1.3 * R2_ctrl (Oster's recommended default)
  R2_max <- min(1.0, 1.3 * R2_ctrl)
  
  # Delta formula from Oster (2019, Journal of Business and Economic Statistics, equation 4):
  # delta = beta_ctrl * (R2_max - R2_ctrl) / 
  #         ((beta_unc - beta_ctrl) * (R2_ctrl - R2_unc))
  num   <- beta_ctrl * (R2_max - R2_ctrl)
  denom <- (beta_unc - beta_ctrl) * (R2_ctrl - R2_unc)
  delta_h1 <- if (abs(denom) > 1e-12) num / denom else NA_real_
  
  # Identified set bound on beta given delta = 1 (selection equally important)
  # beta_star solves beta_star = beta_ctrl - delta * (beta_unc - beta_ctrl) * (R2_max - R2_ctrl) / (R2_ctrl - R2_unc)
  beta_at_delta1 <- beta_ctrl - 1 * (beta_unc - beta_ctrl) * (R2_max - R2_ctrl) / (R2_ctrl - R2_unc)
  
  list(
    R2_unc = R2_unc, R2_ctrl = R2_ctrl, R2_max = R2_max,
    beta_unc = beta_unc, beta_ctrl = beta_ctrl,
    delta = delta_h1, beta_at_delta1 = beta_at_delta1
  )
}, error = function(e) NULL)

if (!is.null(oster_result)) {
  data.frame(
    Statistic = c("Beta H1 uncontrolled (gov_corruption only, after FE)",
                  "Beta H1 controlled (full theory-sparse, after FE)",
                  "R-squared uncontrolled",
                  "R-squared controlled",
                  "R-squared max (1.3 x controlled, capped at 1)",
                  "Oster delta (selection ratio that drives H1 beta to zero)",
                  "Implied beta at delta=1 (equal observed and unobserved selection)"),
    Value = c(round(oster_result$beta_unc, 4),
              round(oster_result$beta_ctrl, 4),
              round(oster_result$R2_unc, 4),
              round(oster_result$R2_ctrl, 4),
              round(oster_result$R2_max, 4),
              round(oster_result$delta, 3),
              round(oster_result$beta_at_delta1, 4))
  ) %>%
    kable(caption = paste0(
      "Table 18b. Oster (2019) bound for unobserved selection on observables on the H1 coefficient. ",
      "Delta is the proportional selection ratio that solves for beta=0; |delta| > 1 ",
      "indicates that unobserved selection would have to be more important than ",
      "observed selection to overturn the H1 result. ",
      "Beta at delta=1 reports the implied bound under equal observed and unobserved selection."
    ))
} else {
  kable(data.frame(Note = "Oster bound estimation failed; see code log."),
        caption = "Table 18b. Oster (2019) bound estimation error.")
}
```

`r if (!is.null(oster_result) && !is.na(oster_result$delta) && abs(oster_result$delta) > 1) sprintf("The Oster delta of %.2f indicates that unobserved selection would need to be roughly %.1f times as important as observed selection to drive the H1 coefficient to zero. By Oster's heuristic |delta| > 1 is reassuring against the most plausible selection-on-unobservables story.", oster_result$delta, abs(oster_result$delta)) else if (!is.null(oster_result) && !is.na(oster_result$delta)) sprintf("The Oster delta of %.2f indicates that unobserved selection of less than the magnitude of observed selection could overturn the H1 result, which is a cautionary signal. The H1 reframe to long-run trend co-movement (Section 5.2) is the substantive response to this fragility, alongside the PMG long-run estimate (Table 26) and the CCEMG common-factor-adjusted estimate (Table 27) which provide alternative identification strategies for the long-run governance-tourism relationship.", oster_result$delta) else "Oster bound could not be computed; selection sensitivity is bounded informally by the country-trends test (Table 18) and the long-run estimators in Tables 26 and 27."`

### Within-country SD ratios — H5 power diagnostic

Table 22 reports within-country standard deviations by income bin. **We surface the actual numbers here and read them as H5 power constraints.** Where the low/high SD ratio exceeds 1.5, the H5 saturation reading cannot be separated from reduced identifying variation in the high-income bin.

```{r tbl-within-sd}
#| label: tbl-within-sd
within_sd_fn <- function(df, var) {
  df %>%
    group_by(Country) %>%
    summarise(sd_w = sd(.data[[var]], na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
    summarise(mean_sd = mean(sd_w, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
    pull(mean_sd)
}
het_vars <- c("gov_corruption", "env_pm25_exp", "soc_internet_users", "soc_unempl_ilo")
hi_data <- dta_clean %>% filter(high_income == 1)
lo_data <- dta_clean %>% filter(high_income == 0)

wsd_table <- data.frame(
  Variable     = het_vars,
  SD_HighIncome  = round(sapply(het_vars, function(v) within_sd_fn(hi_data, v)), 4),
  SD_LowMiddle   = round(sapply(het_vars, function(v) within_sd_fn(lo_data, v)), 4)
) %>%
  mutate(Ratio_LO_HI = round(SD_LowMiddle / SD_HighIncome, 2),
         Note = if_else(Ratio_LO_HI > 1.5,
                        "Low/mid has substantially more variation; saturation indistinguishable from reduced identifying variation",
                        "Variation difference small; saturation interpretation tenable"))
wsd_table %>%
  kable(caption = "Table 22. Within-country standard deviation by income bin (mean across countries). Ratio > 1.5 flags H5 power constraints.")

# Capture for inline narrative
hi_sd_corr <- wsd_table$SD_HighIncome[wsd_table$Variable == "gov_corruption"]
lo_sd_corr <- wsd_table$SD_LowMiddle[wsd_table$Variable == "gov_corruption"]
ratio_corr <- wsd_table$Ratio_LO_HI[wsd_table$Variable == "gov_corruption"]
ratio_inet <- wsd_table$Ratio_LO_HI[wsd_table$Variable == "soc_internet_users"]
```

The within-country SD ratio for `gov_corruption` is `r ratio_corr`, and for `soc_internet_users` it is `r ratio_inet`. The discussion in Section 7 should temper the H5 saturation language for any regressor whose ratio exceeds 1.5, substituting "consistent with both saturation and reduced identifying variation; the data cannot distinguish."
